name: Iris Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Iris. I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not linked to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I cook at Fennel, a plant-based restaurant that's run as a co-op, which means the staff own it together. We do about a hundred covers at lunch and a hundred and thirty at dinner, and I float between the grill and the cold section. My morning starts with an AI app I set up that tells me what's about to go off in the walk-in fridge, so I can turn it into the staff meal or a special. I love that the kitchen is ours, and I hate the dish pit when the porter calls in sick.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about life outside work, and how things are with money.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with my friend Noor, who's a graphic designer, so the rent's split. I've got about three months saved, and I'm not a member-owner of the co-op yet because the buy-in is two thousand pounds. On my days off I do a pop-up supper club about once a month in a friend's bar. I use AI every day, for costing dishes, for menu wording, for working out how much tofu to order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI is a useful kitchen tool and that's all it ever needed to be. I'd post my waste-tracking setup online, because it's genuinely saved us money. People in the trade would ask how to copy it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's fine for me, maybe even good. The co-op isn't going anywhere, my pay is average but steady, and the pop-ups bring in a bit extra. My main worry is just the buy-in money for the co-op.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep cooking at Fennel and keep using the apps to cut waste. I'd put the pop-up money, about two hundred a month, toward the two thousand pound buy-in and aim to become a member by next autumn. I'd maybe teach a couple of other kitchens my waste setup for a small fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit excited even. It's a world I already know how to work in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does becoming a member of the co-op actually change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get a vote on everything, from the menu to the pay rates, and a share of the profit at year end. Last year that was about six hundred pounds each. It's the difference between working somewhere and owning a slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the waste setup saved money. How much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About a fifth of our veg waste, roughly ninety pounds a week. The app reads our stock sheet and flags what's going to turn. Our waste app isn't clever, it's just organised, which kitchens usually aren't.

say: I'd say AI is a **useful kitchen tool** and that's all it needed to be.
I'd share my **waste-tracking setup** online so other kitchens could copy it.
think: I think the **co-op is stable** and my average pay is steady.
I believe my only real worry is raising the **£2,000 buy-in**.
do: Put about **£200 a month** of pop-up money toward the co-op buy-in.
Keep using **waste apps** at Fennel to cut spoiled veg.
Teach other kitchens her **waste setup** for a small fee.
feel: She feels **calm** and a little **excited**, in a world she already understands.
S0.quote: Our waste app isn't clever, it's just organised, which kitchens usually aren't.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **daily** and sees it as plain organisation, not magic.
Her goal is **ownership**: buying into the co-op for a vote and profit share.
The **pop-up supper club** is both side income and a creative outlet.

steps.text: Put pop-up supper club money toward the £2,000 co-op buy-in
Keep running the waste-tracking app at Fennel
Charge other kitchens a small fee to set up waste tracking

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why worker-owned kitchens make sense. If the software saves time, the people who do the work should decide what happens with it. I'd post that and probably get into arguments with chain chefs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think it's good for me. The ordering, costing and rota work is the boring thinking side, and the co-op would hand it to software and keep everyone. My hands are still on the grill for years, because robots spread slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to run the co-op's switch to AI ordering and rotas, which gives me a stronger case for membership. I'd propose that saved hours go into shorter shifts, not fewer staff. And I'd keep the pop-ups going, maybe twice a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, a bit buzzy. I like being the one who sets things up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the kitchen would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gerry, who's sixty and does all our ordering by phone with suppliers he's known for twenty years. If software does the ordering, Gerry (our sixty-year-old orderer) loses the part of the job he's proud of. I'd want him moved to training the young ones, not pushed out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op voted to cut staff instead of shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd lose that vote and argue again next year. That's how it works. But I'd be surprised, because most of us joined Fennel to get away from places that cut staff.

say: I'd say this is why **worker-owned** kitchens make sense.
I'd argue the people who work should decide what to do with **saved time**.
think: I think the **boring thinking work** goes to software and nobody loses their job.
I believe my **grill work** stays human for years, since robots spread slowly.
do: Volunteer to run the co-op's switch to **AI ordering** and rotas.
Propose that saved hours become **shorter shifts**, not fewer staff.
Run the **pop-up** supper club twice a month instead of once.
feel: She feels **mostly calm** and a bit buzzy about leading the setup.
S1.quote: If software does the ordering, Gerry (our sixty-year-old orderer) loses the part of the job he's proud of.
fieldNote: She sees Steady Disruption as an **opportunity**, partly because she's already fluent in the tools.
Her concern goes to an **older colleague** whose pride is tied to phone ordering.
Her trust rests on the **co-op structure** protecting staff.

steps.text: Volunteer to set up AI ordering and rotas at Fennel
Propose to the co-op that saved hours shorten shifts
Run the supper club pop-up twice a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this needs public ownership of some of it, or at least a big tax. If one company owns the AI that runs every kitchen, that's a disaster. I'd go loud online and I'd push the co-op network to make a statement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the thinking side of the kitchen changes overnight, and I'm ready for that. The scary part is 2031, when cooking robots arrive and I've only got three months of savings. Fennel would survive if the co-op bought the robots itself, but I'm not a member yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get the buy-in paid in the first year, even if it means skipping holidays, so I'm an owner before the robots come. I'd push the co-op to save up for its own cooking robot rather than lose to chains that buy them. And I'd vote and campaign for an AI tax that funds people like Gerry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited about some of it, but three years isn't much when you've only got three months saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your supper clubs in this world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think they get more valuable, honestly. When every chain meal is made by a machine, people pay for a person cooking in front of them. I'd charge more and do them weekly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd skip holidays. What's the trip you'd cancel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Noor and I booked Lisbon for next spring, about four hundred each. I'd cancel it and put the money into the buy-in. Noor would be cross, but she's worried about AI in design too, so she'd get it.

say: I'd say AGI needs **public ownership** or at least a big tax.
I'd push the **co-op network** to make a public statement.
think: I think the kitchen's **thinking work** changes overnight, and I'm ready for that.
I believe **2031 robots** are the real threat, with only three months saved.
do: Pay the co-op **buy-in** within the first year by cancelling a trip.
Push Fennel to save for its **own robot** rather than lose to chains.
Campaign for an **AI tax** that funds older kitchen workers.
feel: She feels **anxious**, excited about parts of it but short on savings.
S2.quote: When every chain meal is made by a machine, people pay for a person cooking in front of them.
fieldNote: She splits AGI cleanly: **thinking work** now, which she welcomes, and robots in 2031, which she fears.
Becoming an **owner** before robots arrive is her central defence.
Her **supper clubs** become a hedge built on human presence.

steps.text: Cancel the Lisbon trip and pay the co-op buy-in
Propose Fennel saves for its own cooking robot
Campaign for an AI tax that funds kitchen workers
Run the supper club weekly at higher prices

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I'd say with the fast one, but with more room for planning. Five years is enough for co-ops to get organised and buy robots together. I'd want the co-op network to set up a shared fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Personally, it's manageable. By 2031 I'd be a member. By 2034 I'd rather own a share in the kitchen robots than be replaced by them. The thinking side I'd already be running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, I'd pay the buy-in and start a short evening course on kitchen equipment and automation at the tech college. I'd join the co-op's planning group. And I'd grow the supper club into a proper side business with a booking page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than anxious. I can see the path, but a lot depends on the co-op voting the right way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a course on kitchen equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when the robots arrive, someone has to set them up, clean them and fix the small stuff. I'd rather that be me than an engineer from the company who charges ninety pounds an hour. It's eight weeks, Tuesdays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the co-op says no to buying robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then Fennel probably slowly loses to the chains on price. I'd stay and fight for it, but I'd also be glad I'd built up the supper club. That's my backup.

say: I'd say five years lets co-ops **organise** and buy robots together.
I'd push the co-op network to set up a **shared fund**.
think: I think I'd be a **member** by 2031 and part-own the robots by 2034.
I believe I'd already be **running** the thinking side of the kitchen.
do: Pay the **co-op buy-in** in the first year.
Take an eight-week evening course on **kitchen equipment** and automation.
Grow the supper club into a **side business** with a booking page.
feel: She feels **uneasy** rather than anxious, since much depends on co-op votes.
S3.quote: By 2034 I'd rather own a share in the kitchen robots than be replaced by them.
fieldNote: Five years turns her fear into a **plan**: membership, then shared robots.
She wants to be the one who **maintains** the machines, not a contractor.
Her backup is the **supper club**, showing she hedges even within her ideals.

steps.text: Pay the £2,000 co-op buy-in this year
Take an eight-week kitchen automation course on Tuesdays
Push Fennel to plan buying cooking robots by 2034
Set up a booking page for the supper club

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it that's on us. Every co-op and union should have a plan by 2030. I'd write a post about it and send it round the co-op network.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's honestly fine. I'd be thirty-nine or so when cooking robots come, already an owner, maybe running Fennel's menu and the machines. The supper club could be a real business by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay the buy-in, then over a few years do the equipment course and a food business course. I'd save some of my profit share every year toward opening a second co-op site. And I'd keep using AI to plan everything, because that's already how I work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, even. Ten years is enough to build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that still bothers you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people who don't have a co-op. Most cooks work for chains or owners who'll keep the robot savings for themselves. I'd be fine, and me being fine is not the same as cooks being fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a second co-op site look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller, maybe forty covers, with a robot doing the line and three of us doing menus, guests and events. Owned by whoever works there. That's my dream, honestly.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and wasting it would be on us.
I'd urge every **co-op and union** to have a plan by 2030.
think: I think I'd be an **owner** by the time cooking robots arrive.
I believe the **supper club** could become a real business in ten years.
do: Pay the buy-in and later take a **food business course**.
Save part of each year's **profit share** toward a second co-op site.
Keep using **AI tools** to plan menus, ordering and events.
feel: She feels **calm** and **hopeful**, with time to build something.
S4.quote: I'd be fine, and me being fine is not the same as cooks being fine.
fieldNote: She's **secure** in this picture because of ownership and early skills.
Her **progressive** concern shows: she worries for cooks without a co-op.
Her dream is a small **robot-assisted** co-op site owned by its workers.

steps.text: Save part of each profit share toward a second co-op site
Take a food business course over the next few years
Grow the supper club into a regular business

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I wouldn't be an owner yet and I've only got three months saved. What would help is a way to get into the co-op faster, like a loan scheme for kitchen workers to buy in. And a tax on AI that actually reaches people like Gerry.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about food itself. If robots cook everything, someone still decides what's worth eating. That's the part of cooking I'd fight to keep human.

headlineQuote: If robots cook everything, someone still decides what's worth eating.
portrait: Iris is a **27-year-old** cook at a worker-owned plant-based restaurant, sharing a flat with her friend Noor.
She uses **AI daily** for waste tracking and costing, and runs a monthly supper club.
She stays **calm** in the flat and steady worlds, seeing AI as plain organisation.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** because she's not yet a co-op owner and has three months saved.
Her answer to robots is **ownership**: buy in, share the machines, keep the creative work human.
biggestWorry: She fears **AGI by 2028** most, arriving before she's a co-op owner.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **loan scheme** helping kitchen workers buy into co-ops.
She also wants an **AI tax** that reaches older kitchen workers.
